body.p: Claims 1-20 are pending. Claims 1-2, 4-11, and 14-18 are rejected and claims 3, 12- 13, and 19-20 are objected to. Claims 1, 10, and 17 are amended. No new matter has been added.
Claim Rejection - 35 USC s 102
Claims 1, 10, and 17 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. f102(a)(2) as being anticipated by Holland (WO 2021216060 A1). This rejection is respectfully traversed.
It is respectfully submitted that Holland does not disclose the recitations of claim 1. Holland does not disclose:
applying the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding the first user to determine
that a type of the real-world environment includes one of an
indoor environment and an outdoor environment

as is recited in claim 1. Rather, Holland describes determining an acoustic presentation to be output to a user via headphones. The "acoustic presentation" is not the "type of the real-world environment" including "one of an indoor environment and an outdoor environment", as is recited in claim 1. Figure 2A of Holland is reproduced below.
[00144] Referring generally to FIGS. 2A-F, the AI systems 200
and associated machine- learned models can cooperatively
work to intelligently curate a user's acoustic environment 206.
For example, event(s) 204 can be analyzed to determine an
urgency 246 of the event(s) 204. The event(s) 204 can be
summarized based on the semantic content 234 of the event(s) 204. Audio signal(s) associated with the event(s) 204 can be
generated by the AI system 200. The AI system 200 can
determine a particular time to present the audio signal(s) to the
user, such as at a convenient time The audio signal(s) can be incorporated into the user's acoustic environment 206, such
as music playing on a user's smartphone, at the particular
time.
(Emphasis Added)
Also, Figures 9A-9D of Holland are reproduced below.
[00150] Referring now to FIGS. 9A-D, an example "loop"
intervention tactic is depicted. For example, as depicted in FIG.
9A, an acoustic environment 910 is shown. A portion 912 (e.g.,
a slice) of the acoustic environment 910 can be selected. For example, the portion 912 can be an upcoming portion of the
acoustic environment 910 at which an audio signal associated
with one or more events 920 is to be incorporated into the
acoustic environment 910. As depicted in FIG. 9B, when the portion 912A is played (e.g., when the acoustic environment
910 reaches the first portion), the audio signal associated with
the one or more events 920 can be incorporated into the
acoustic environment 910 by playing the audio signal 920. As shown in FIG. 9C, upon completing playing the portion 912A,
a second portion 912B can be played while the audio signal 920
is played. Upon completing playing the portion 912B, a third
portion 912C can be played while the audio signal 920 is
played. Successive portions 912 can similarly be repeatedly
played until the completion of the audio signal 920. In this way,
the loop intervention tactic can hold and repeatedly play a portion 912 of the acoustic environment 910 by repeatedly
looping the portion 912 of the acoustic environment 910.
(Emphasis Added)

As such, in Holland, "audio signal(s) associated with the event(s) 204" are determined and generated by the AI system 200. The "audio signal(s)" are not "the type of the real-world environment" including "one of an indoor environment and an outdoor environment", as is recited in claim 1. There is no determination in Holland that the type of the real-world environment" includes "one of an indoor environment and an outdoor environment", as is recited in claim 1. Hence, for at least the reasons set forth above, claim 1 is submitted to be novel in view of Holland.
Also, claim 10 is submitted to be novel over Holland. For example, for the same reasons set forth above, Holland fails to disclose:
a processor configured to:

apply the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding a user to determine that a type of the real-world environment includes one of an indoor environment and an outdoor environment
as is recited in claim 10. Thus, claim 10 is submitted be novel in view of Holland.
Moreover, claim 17 is submitted to be novel over Holland. As an example, for the same reasons set forth above, Holland fails to disclose: a server configured to:

apply the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding a user to determine that a type of the real-world environment includes one of an indoor environment and an outdoor environment
as is recited in claim 17. Thus, claim 17 is submitted be novel in view of Holland.
Therefore, it is respectfully submitted that the section 102 rejection of claims 1, 10,
and 17 be withdrawn.
First Claim Rejection - 35 USC § 103
Claims 2, 11, and 18 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as being unpatentable over Holland and further in view of Chien (US 2023/0147573). This rejection is respectfully traversed.

Claim 2 depends from independent claim 1, claim 11 depends from independent claim 10, and claim 18 depends from independent claim 17. It is respectfully submitted that the combination of Holland and Chien does not disclose or suggest the recitations of claim 1. For example, the combination of Holland and Chien fails to teach:
applying the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding the first user to determine
that a type of the real-world environment includes one of an
indoor environment and an outdoor environment as is recited in claim 1.
As another example, the combination of Holland and Chien fails to teach:
a processor configured to:

apply the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding a user to determine that a type of the real-world environment includes one of an indoor environment and an outdoor environment
as is recited in claim 10.
As yet another example, the combination of Holland and Chien fails to teach:
a server configured to:

apply the AI model to audio data captured from the real-world environment surrounding a user to determine that a type of the real-world environment includes one of an indoor environment and an outdoor environment
as is recited in claim 17.

Holland is explained above. Moreover, Chien is not cited to cure the deficiencies in Holland. Rather, Chien is cited to disclose "extracted audio features from one or more representative audio samples, such as low-level audio features, including: spectral centroid, spectral roll-off, signal energy, mel-frequency cepstrum coefficients (MFCCs), linear predictor coefficients (LPC), line spectral frequency (LSF) coefficients, loudness coefficients, sharpness of loudness coefficients, spread of loudness coefficients, octave band signal intensities" (see Office Action, page 7). Hence, for the reasons set forth above, the independent claims 1, 10, and 17 and the respective dependent claims 2, 11, and 18 are submitted to be nonobvious in view of the combination of Holland and Chien.
Therefore, it is respectfully requested that the section 103 rejection of claims 2, 11, and 18 be withdrawn.

Claim 15 depends from independent claim 10. It is respectfully submitted that the combination of Holland and Yeung does not disclose or suggest the recitations of claim 1. For example, the combination of Holland and Yeung fails to teach:

receiving video data captured from a plurality of different
cameras at an event, the video data comprising a plurality of video images captured from each of the plurality of different
cameras; performing image recognition on at least a portion of
